text: Late that night, as Bernice passed her aunts door, she heard her own name and stopped, unable to resist listening to the conversation inside. <break time="0.8s" /> Marjorie was complaining to her mother that Bernice was hopeless, and that no boy would ever take an interest in such a dull, awkward girl. <break time="0.8s" /> Missus Harvey tried to defend her niece, but Marjorie replied that being nice and polite meant nothing to boys if a girl had no charm. <break time="0.8s" /> The next morning, Bernice accused her cousin of being cruel, and she threatened to go home to Eau Claire at once if she was not wanted. <break time="0.8s" /> Instead of apologizing, Marjorie coolly answered that her cousin was free to leave, since she had made no effort to be pleasant company. <break time="0.8s" /> When Bernice spoke of the gentle, womanly girls in Little Women, Marjorie laughed and declared that such old fashioned ideals no longer belonged in the modern world. <break time="0.8s" /> Shaken but secretly impressed, Bernice swallowed her pride and asked, Will you tell me what is wrong with me, and how I can change it. <break time="0.8s" /> Marjorie agreed to help her, but only on one condition, that Bernice would do exactly what she was told without arguing or asking why.
